lede: Rehab after ACL reconstruction that follows your surgeon's protocol, from getting the knee straight again to rebuilding the strength and control needed for sport.
what_it_is: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) runs diagonally through the middle of the knee. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons explains that it keeps the shinbone from sliding forward under the thighbone and steadies the knee when you twist. A torn ACL does not heal well on its own, so in a reconstruction the surgeon replaces it with a tendon graft, usually taken from your own patellar, hamstring or quadriceps tendon, or from a donor.

Surgery gives the knee a new ligament, but the graft has to mature and the muscles around the knee lose strength quickly after injury and surgery. Rehab rebuilds full knee straightening, quadriceps and hamstring strength, balance and landing control. The AAOS says return to sport depends on progress, strength and movement quality rather than the calendar alone, so your therapist works through your surgeon's protocol and tests readiness at each step.
symptoms: Swelling in the knee after surgery
Quadriceps weakness and difficulty tightening the thigh
Pain at the graft site or the front of the knee
Limping and reliance on crutches early on
Poor balance and low confidence when cutting, jumping or landing
causes: A complete ACL tear, which the AAOS notes is the most common type
Sports or jobs that involve pivoting, turning or hard cutting
A knee that keeps giving way during daily activities
Combined injuries to the ACL and other knee structures such as the meniscus
Injury from changing direction quickly, stopping suddenly or landing poorly from a jump
Direct contact or collision in sports

how_therapy_helps.intro: The American Physical Therapy Association's clinical practice guideline on knee ligament sprain, published in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy, recommends moving the knee within 1 week after ACL reconstruction to restore motion and reduce pain. It also recommends supervised exercise in the clinic paired with a progressive home program, strengthening started within 4 to 6 weeks and continued 2 to 3 times a week for 6 to 10 months, and neuromuscular training combined with strength work. Your surgeon's protocol sets the order and timing.
methods: Exercises that prioritize getting the knee fully straight and gradually restoring bend, which the APTA guideline recommends starting within the first week.
Weight bearing and non weight bearing exercises progressed over months, as the APTA guideline describes, to rebuild thigh strength.
Walking practice as you move off crutches, following your surgeon's weight bearing instructions.
Balance, landing and movement control drills that the APTA guideline recommends pairing with strength work.
A gradual return to jogging, cutting and jumping in later phases, introduced only when your surgeon and therapist agree.
Strength comparisons and single leg hop tests, which the APTA guideline lists for checking side to side differences and readiness.

first_visit: The first appointment runs about an hour, and you begin treatment during it. Your therapist reviews your surgeon's protocol, graft type, brace settings and weight bearing status, and asks about any meniscus work done at the same time. They measure swelling, how fully the knee straightens and bends, and how well you can tighten the quadriceps. They watch you walk, check the incisions, and set up a home program focused on motion and swelling.
recovery: ACL rehab takes months, and sources describe a range. Johns Hopkins Medicine outlines three broad phases: roughly 6 to 8 weeks to control swelling and regain motion, 2 to 4 months to rebuild strength and start light jogging, and 4 to 8 months for a graduated return to full activity. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says most patients return to full sports within 6 to 12 months, and Mayo Clinic notes athletes often need a year or more. Readiness is judged by testing, and your surgeon gives final clearance.
self_care: Keep your leg elevated on pillows several times a day in the first week, as MedlinePlus advises.
Wear your brace as instructed and do not change its settings yourself.
Use crutches and bear weight only as your surgeon allows.
Practice gently tightening your thigh muscle and working on straightening the knee, if your discharge exercises include them.
Avoid heating pads on the knee and keep the dressing dry.
see_a_doctor: Swelling or pain in your calf, which can signal a blood clot
Chest pain or sudden trouble breathing, which needs emergency care (call 911)
Fever above 101°F, or redness, warmth or drainage at an incision
Blood soaking through the bandage that pressure does not stop
A foot or toes that look discolored or feel cool
Pain that your medicine does not relieve, or a new feeling of the knee giving way

faqs.q: When does physical therapy start after ACL surgery?
faqs.a: Therapy usually starts soon after surgery. The APTA clinical practice guideline recommends moving the knee within 1 week after ACL reconstruction to improve range of motion and reduce pain. MedlinePlus describes formal physical therapy often starting 1 to 2 weeks after surgery. Your surgeon decides the start date and early limits, so bring your protocol to your first visit.

faqs.q: How long does ACL rehab take?
faqs.a: ACL rehab typically spans many months. The APTA guideline describes strengthening 2 to 3 times a week for 6 to 10 months. MedlinePlus notes formal therapy often lasts 2 to 6 months, with return to full activity commonly 4 to 6 months or longer, while the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons cites 6 to 12 months for full sports. Your progress and your surgeon's protocol set the pace.

faqs.q: Why is getting my knee straight so important after ACL surgery?
faqs.a: Full knee straightening lets you walk normally and stand without strain. The APTA guideline recommends early mobilization partly to reduce the risk of losing knee extension, and the AAOS lists stiffness among possible complications. That is why early rehab focuses on straightening the knee alongside controlling swelling, within the limits your surgeon sets.

faqs.q: When can I return to sports after ACL reconstruction?
faqs.a: The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says most patients return to full sports within 6 to 12 months, and Mayo Clinic notes athletes often need a year or more. The AAOS lists criteria such as no pain or swelling, full range of motion, and fully restored strength, endurance and function. Your surgeon gives final clearance after testing your knee.

faqs.q: Do I need a brace to play sports after ACL reconstruction?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons states that a functional brace is not required after a successful ACL reconstruction, though some athletes feel more secure wearing one. The APTA guideline advises that clinicians discuss your preferences, since evidence exists for and against bracing. Ask your surgeon what they recommend for your sport.

faqs.q: What are hop tests after ACL surgery?
faqs.a: Hop tests are short jumping tasks on one leg, such as a single hop for distance, a crossover hop, a triple hop and a timed 6 meter hop. The APTA guideline recommends tests like these to measure side to side differences, track progress and help judge readiness to return to activity. They are done later in rehab, once your surgeon allows jumping.

notes_for_reviewer: Return to sport timelines differ across sources. MedlinePlus says 4 to 6 months to full activity, Johns Hopkins says 4 to 8 months for phase 3, AAOS says 6 to 12 months, and Mayo Clinic says a year or more for athletes. The page presents them as a range and does not pick one. Many current sports medicine protocols lean toward 9 months or later, so consider whether to say so.

The 2017 APTA/JOSPT guideline also recommends neuromuscular electrical stimulation for 6 to 8 weeks, cryotherapy, and possible use of CPM after ACL reconstruction. These were left out of the methods because they are not on the clinic's approved services list. Add NMES if the clinic offers it.

Johns Hopkins states that about 85 percent of patients return to their previous activity level. This was not used, because the brief prohibits outcome rate claims that could read as clinic promises. Use it only with clear attribution if wanted.
ICD-10 Z47.89 is a general orthopedic aftercare code. Billing may use a different code based on the surgeon's documentation. Please confirm.
Check whether a newer ACL guideline revision exists. The JOSPT knee ligament sprain guideline found and read is the 2017 revision.
